title: Practice: loss functions & metrics for regression
intro: The practice assignment, worked out: MSE, RMSE, MAE and R² from scratch with complete answers you can run in the browser, a regression line to drag with sliders, and an explanation of why one loss fits better than another. Based on the course assignment Loss functions & metrics.

blocks.html:
Before we dive into loss functions and metrics, let's line up the bigger picture. Machine learning comes in three categories: supervised learning (learning from labelled data), unsupervised learning (finding structure without labels) and reinforcement learning (learning by trial-and-error with rewards).

Only in supervised learning do you need labelled data \( (X, y) \) — and precisely that category knows two forms of applications: regression and classification. The difference lies in the measurement level of the target variable: in regression \( y \) is quantitative (a number, like a price or a temperature); in classification \( y \) is qualitative (a category, like spam/not spam).

Thinking questions (from the assignment):

  • What are the three categories of machine learning?
  • In which of those three do you need labelled data?
  • What are the two forms of applications in that category?
  • What are the measurement levels of the target variables in each of those two forms?

sections.title: Loss functions for regression: the theory

blocks.html: The three most used loss functions for a regression problem are Mean Squared Error (MSE), Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) and Mean Absolute Error (MAE). All three measure how far the predictions \( \hat{y} \) are from the true values \( y \), but each in its own way — and you feel that difference especially when there are outliers in the data.

blocks.label: Mean Squared Error
blocks.caption: Squares every error and averages: large errors count extra heavily.

blocks.label: Root Mean Squared Error
blocks.caption: The square root of the MSE — back in the same unit as the target, which makes interpretation easier.

blocks.label: Mean Absolute Error
blocks.caption: Takes the absolute error: more robust against outliers, but harder to derive.

blocks.html: The symbols: \( N \) is the number of data points, \( i \) is the running index over those points, \( y_i \) is the true target value of point \( i \) and \( \hat{y}_i \) ("y-hat") is the predicted target value of the model for that same point.
Assignment: explain in your own words what \( N \), \( i \), \( y_i \) and \( \hat{y}_i \) are — and why the MSE is more sensitive to outliers than the MAE.

sections.title: Exercise: predicting the price of a car

blocks.html:
You run a linear regression with three feature variables and one target variable:

  • X1 — age of the car (in years): 1, 3, 4, 7, 9
  • X2 — mileage (in 10,000 km): 5, 12, 15, 23, 30
  • X3 — number of previous owners: 1, 2, 1, 3, 2
  • Y — price of the car (in € 1000): 18, 12, 10, 6, 4

After training you arrive at the parameters \( b_0 = 20 \), \( b_1 = -1 \), \( b_2 = -0.5 \) and \( b_3 = -2 \). The prediction equation is therefore:

blocks.label: car price prediction
blocks.caption: Fill in the feature values for each car and you get the predicted price.

blocks.html: Questions (from the assignment): (1) compute the predictions for each of the five cars; (2) then compute the MSE, RMSE and MAE of the model. The worked solution below is the complete answer — press Run to execute the code and see all results right in your browser.

blocks.caption: worked solution — the answer
blocks.source:
import numpy as np

X = np.array([[1,  5, 1],
              [3, 12, 2],
              [4, 15, 1],
              [7, 23, 3],
              [9, 30, 2]], dtype=float)
y = np.array([18, 12, 10, 6, 4], dtype=float)
b0, b1, b2, b3 = 20.0, -1.0, -0.5, -2.0

# 1) predictions
y_hat = b0 + b1*X[:, 0] + b2*X[:, 1] + b3*X[:, 2]
print('predictions:', y_hat)

# 2) loss metrics
mse_waarde  = np.mean((y - y_hat)**2)
rmse_waarde = np.sqrt(mse_waarde)
mae_waarde  = np.mean(np.abs(y - y_hat))
print('MSE :', round(mse_waarde, 2))
print('RMSE:', round(rmse_waarde, 2))
print('MAE :', round(mae_waarde, 2))

# extra: explained variance
r2_waarde = 1 - np.sum((y - y_hat)**2) / np.sum((y - y.mean())**2)
print('R2  :', round(r2_waarde, 2), '(negative = worse than predicting the mean!)')

sections.title: Worked out: MSE, RMSE and MAE from scratch

blocks.html: The functions from scratch, fully worked out. Each function takes two parameters: the true target values and the predicted target values (which can come from any regression model). At the bottom of the cell the code checks itself against the expected values from the assignment.

blocks.caption: worked solution — the answer

blocks.html: The metric usually used for regression is the explained variance, \( R^2 \). It is a statistical measure of how much of the variance in the dependent variable (target) is explained by the independent variables (features). Here too we see the difference between the predicted target value \( \hat{y} \) and the mean of the actual target values \( \bar{y} \):

blocks.label: explained variance
blocks.caption: The denominator measures the spread around the mean; the numerator the spread around your predictions.

rows: the model fits every data point perfectly
no better than simply predicting the mean

blocks.html: A value close to 1 means many data points sit close to the regression line; a value close to 0 means the line explains little. And as you saw in the car-price exercise: negative is possible too — your model then performs worse than a model that just always predicts the mean.

blocks.caption: worked solution — the answer
blocks.source:
import numpy as np

def r2_score(y_true, y_pred):
    # numerator: spread around the predictions (the model's errors)
    ss_res = np.sum((y_true - y_pred)**2)
    # denominator: spread around the mean (the naive prediction)
    ss_tot = np.sum((y_true - y_true.mean())**2)
    return 1 - ss_res / ss_tot

# check with the values from the assignment
y_true = np.array([3.0, -0.5, 2.0, 7.0])
y_pred = np.array([2.5,  0.0, 2.0, 8.0])

print('r2_score:', r2_score(y_true, y_pred))  # expected 0.9486081370449679

sections.title: Visualising: does the line fit the data?

blocks.html: Below you see three datasets, each with one feature variable and a linear model \( y_{pred} = b_0 + b_1 x \), where \( b_0 \) is the y-intercept and \( b_1 \) the slope. Drag the sliders to fit the line and try to find the best loss and the best R² for each dataset.

blocks.title: Dataset A — clean, linear data
blocks.subtitle: Slide b0 and b1 until the line runs through the points. Best fit roughly: b1 ≈ 1.9, b0 ≈ 1.7.

blocks.title: Dataset B — with one big outlier
blocks.subtitle: One point deviates far (a single 24 while the rest sit around the line). Notice how the MSE mindset drags the line towards that point.

blocks.title: Dataset C — curved (quadratic) data
blocks.subtitle: However you place the line: a straight line cannot fit a curve. R² stays low — adapt the model (e.g. add x² as a feature), not just the line.

blocks.html:
Exercises (from the assignment):

  • Which loss function would you use for dataset A, B and C — and why? (Think of the outlier in B.)
  • What are the best loss values you can find for each of the three datasets?
  • What are the best R² values per dataset?
  • Which parameter values (b0 and b1) go with them?
  • How would you improve R² for dataset C?

With multiple features the equation becomes \( y_{pred} = b_0 + b_1 x_1 + b_2 x_2 + \cdots + b_n x_n \) — a plane instead of a line. The car-price exercise above is exactly such a case with three features.
